newsitem.title: PERU: Japan urges caution as Peru rebels shoot at police.
newsitem.headline: Japan urges caution as Peru rebels shoot at police.

text.p: Japan repeated calls for restraint in Peru's six-week hostage crisis on Tuesday after Marxist guerrillas holding 72 captives fired on police staging a show of force outside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

"I'm worried if the terrorists have been irritated over moves of the (Peruvian) special forces. We are asking for care to be taken about such moves," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.
Several bullets struck a police armoured vehicle on Monday afternoon as security forces staged the largest display of strength since the rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17.
The shots came after Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels shouted at police aboard the armoured cars and the officers responded with obscene gestures.
"One bullet ricocheted off the front window and the others hit the back (of the vehicle)," one policeman told Reuters.
The gunfire sent the police scurrying for cover, pointing their assault rifles and machine guns up at the building.
It was the first time gunfire has endangered anyone in the hostage drama. On previous occasions, the rebels have fired warning shots into the air in response to police manoeuvres.
Police officers said they had orders not to shoot back.
Even after the shooting, security forces continued their manoeuvres in an apparent attempt to unnerve and crack the resolve of the estimated 15 rebels holding the hostages.

About 200 special forces officers and four armoured vehicles paraded five times around the diplomatic compound to the accompaniment of military march music blasted from speakers. A police helipcopter circled overhead.
The armed display came despite the calls from Tokyo to tone down such tactics to avoid unsettling the hostages.
Police have thrown stones and garbage into the diplomatic compound, flown helicopters overhead and trained machine guns on the house, moves the guerrillas considered a provocation.
The MRTA's international spokesman said the police activity indicated the site would be stormed. He warned that an attack would unleash a backlash from the rebel movement.

"If the residence is stormed, the situation will intensify and become much worse. All across Peru, armed commandos of the MRTA are ready to carry out attacks on economic and political targets," MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco said in an interview with Germany's Junge Welt daily published on Monday.
"The deaths of Tupac Amaru fighters would escalate the conflict across the country," he added in the interview, which was posted on the MRTA's Internet web page.
President Alberto Fujimori, whose brother, Pedro, is among the captives, insisted police moves were not a prelude to an assault and that he was seeking a negotiated solution.

Fujimori's point man in the crisis, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, said a site had been selected for eventual negotiations to end the standoff and a bullet proof vehicle was ready to take MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa to the talks.
And in an apparent goodwill gesture, Palermo told a news conference that Catholic clergymen would form part of a commission to ensure jailed MRTA rebels are fairly treated.
But he gave no clue as to how the government hoped to end the deadlock over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades which Fujimori has refused to discuss.

The guerrillas, who take the name for their movement from an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, orginally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence.

They released most in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
